spec.full_target: Let n,m be positive integers; u:R^n×(0,∞)→R^m jointly smooth and q∈R^m have Euclidean norm one. Assume |u(x,r)|=1; for each (x,r) there is a∈R with u_tt−Δ_xu=a u; and on each compact interval J⊂(0,∞), u=q outside a compact C_J uniformly for r∈J. Define e(x,r)=|u_t|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|² and E(r)=∫_{R^n}e(x,r)dx, Lebesgue measure, Euclidean norms. Prove e(·,r) is Lebesgue integrable for each r>0, E is differentiable for each r>0, and E'(r)=0.
spec.conclusion: For every r>0, e(·,r) is Lebesgue integrable, E is differentiable at r, and E'(r)=0.

hypotheses.statement: For all x∈R^n,r>0 there exists a∈R such that u_tt(x,r)-Δ_xu(x,r)=a u(x,r), with componentwise Δ_x.
For each compact interval J⊂(0,∞), there is compact C_J⊂R^n such that u(x,r)=q for x∉C_J and r∈J.

definitions.definition: E(r)=Lebesgue integral over R^n of e(x,r)

calculations: Finite Euclidean inner-product and finite-sum identities and differentiation of smooth functions. FTC, compactness, uniform continuity and iterated integration are justified in the inference, not treated as trusted primitives.

primitives.meaning: Real field, topology, order, and Lebesgue measure.
Euclidean space with inner product and Lebesgue measure.

propositions.statement: For all x∈R^n,r>0 there exists a∈R such that u_tt(x,r)-Δ_xu(x,r)=a u(x,r), with componentwise Δ_x.
For each compact interval J⊂(0,∞), there is compact C_J⊂R^n such that u(x,r)=q for x∉C_J and r∈J.
For every r>0, e(·,r) is Lebesgue integrable, E is differentiable at r, and E'(r)=0.

locals.type: compact interval in (0,∞) with r0 in its interior
locals.declaration: Choose J after the existence fact F001.
Choose the compact set supplied by H003 for J.
Choose B after the existence fact F002.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary r0>0. Choose δ with 0<δ<r0 and set J=[r0−δ,r0+δ]; thus there exists a compact interval in (0,∞) with r0 in its interior, recorded as F001.

produces.statement: There exists a compact interval J⊂(0,∞) with r0 in its interior.

argument.text: Choose J using F001. H003 applied to this compact interval supplies compact C_J and the stated uniform equality. Compactness of C_J implies boundedness, so a closed coordinate box B containing it exists; record this as F002. On the open complement of C_J, u=q for all times in J, so its spatial and time first derivatives vanish there. By continuity they vanish also at boundary points of C_J. Hence e(·,s) is continuous, zero off C_J and bounded on C_J, and therefore Lebesgue integrable for every s∈J.

produces.statement: There exists a closed coordinate box B⊂R^n containing C_J.

argument.text: Choose B by F002. For s∈J, E(s)=∫_B e(x,s)dx since e vanishes outside C_J⊂B. On B×J, e_s is continuous and uniformly continuous. For sufficiently small nonzero h with r0+h∈J, the one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus gives (e(x,r0+h)−e(x,r0))/h=∫_0^1 e_s(x,r0+θh)dθ. Uniform continuity implies these quotients converge uniformly in x∈B to e_s(x,r0). B has finite measure, so the difference between their integrals and ∫_B e_s(x,r0)dx is at most measure(B) times the uniform error, tending to zero. Thus E is differentiable at r0 and E'(r0)=∫_B e_s(x,r0)dx. Differentiating the finite sum gives e_s=2u_t·u_tt+2Σ_j u_j·∂_j u_t, where u_j=∂_j u.

For each coordinate j, f_j(x)=u_t(x,r0)·u_j(x,r0) is smooth and supported in C_J. Its derivative ∂_j f_j=(∂_j u_t)·u_j+u_t·u_jj is continuous and compactly supported, hence absolutely integrable. Choose a coordinate interval containing C_J in its interior. For each fixed choice of the other coordinates, the one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus gives integral in coordinate j of ∂_j f_j equal to the endpoint difference of f_j, which is zero. Fubini is applicable because ∂_j f_j is absolutely integrable; iterating the integral gives ∫_{R^n}∂_j f_j=0. Therefore ∫(∂_j u_t)·u_j=−∫u_t·u_jj. Summing the finite set of identities yields E'(r0)=2∫_{R^n}u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)dx.

Differentiating |u(x,r)|²=1 in time gives u·u_t=0. By H002, at each x there is a real a with u_tt−Δ_xu=a u. Consequently u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=a(u_t·u)=0 pointwise, so the integral expression for E'(r0) is zero.
Since r0 was arbitrary, the integrability, differentiability, and vanishing derivative established at r0 hold for every positive time. No assertion at the endpoint zero is used.
